source_of_candidates: docs/nemad-paper-check.json: the three nulls a first reader found wrong

candidates.lead: Testardi et al., Phys. Rev. 154, 399 (1967), DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.154.399 (elastic moduli of A15 compounds; its abstract calls Nb3Ge an A-15 superconductor with Tc about 5-7 K). Bulk A15 Nb3Ge is often Ge-deficient; check the composition condition carefully.

Phys. Rev. B 61, 15450 (2000), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.61.15450, arXiv cond-mat/0003077: YBa2Cu3O6+k pairs with 0.28 <= k <= 0.32 studied by resistivity; k = 0.32 reported as the lower limit of a superconducting ortho-II phase.

Matsuishi et al., Phys. Rev. B 89, 094510 (2014), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.89.094510, arXiv 1312.6747: SmFeAs1-yPyO1-xHx; Sec. III.B reports Tc = 4 K for y = 0.53, x = 0.15 from resistivity (2 GPa used only in synthesis).

readerA.quote: "This unusual behavior does not occur for the isostructural compounds V3Ge and Nb3Ge, which have comparatively low transition temperatures (Tc~5-7 °K)."
readerA.page_table_or_figure: Abstract, p. 399. The full text is behind the APS paywall: the abstract page and the PDF both asked for login (PDF returned 401), so I could not read the body, tables or figures.
readerA.phase_or_sample: Polycrystalline A15 'Nb3Ge'. The formula is a label or nominal composition. The abstract gives no analysed Ge content for the A15 phase.
readerA.tc_criterion: Not stated in the abstract. The abstract gives one shared approximate range (~5-7 K) for V3Ge and Nb3Ge together, not a separate Tc for Nb3Ge.
readerA.measurement_method: Elastic moduli measured against temperature on polycrystalline A15 samples. The abstract does not say how Tc was determined.
readerA.synthesis_conditions: Not stated in the abstract. The samples are polycrystalline bulk, made at Bell Telephone Laboratories.
readerA.note:
Verdict: not confirmed. Neither branch of the rule is met.

(1) Testardi et al. 1967 (DOI checked in Crossref: Phys. Rev. 154(2), 399-401) is a bulk, ambient-pressure study. However, I could read only its abstract. That abstract gives only the formula label 'Nb3Ge' with a shared Tc of ~5-7 K. It gives no measured composition, so it does not show 25.0 +/- 0.15 at.% Ge.

(2) The primary metallurgy rules out bulk A15 at 25 at.% Ge. Jorda, Flukiger and Muller, 'The phase diagram of the niobium-germanium system', J. Less-Common Met. 62, 25 (1978), DOI 10.1016/0022-5088(78)90013-9. I read its abstract on the ScienceDirect page; they used microprobe analysis and DTA up to 2200 C. Quote: "the Ge-rich limit of this phase varies with temperature from 20 +/- 1 at.% Ge at 1600 C to 23 +/- 1 at.% Ge at 1865 C, the eutectic temperature. It is thus shown that the stoichiometric composition Nb3Ge is not reached in this system."

(3) Matthias et al., Phys. Rev. 139, A1501 (1965), DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.139.A1501. I read its abstract via OpenAlex. Quote: the Nb-Ge A15 compound "normally forms with excess Nb, has a transition temperature of 6.9 K". Splat-quenched samples made with excess Ge reached up to 17 K, which the authors attribute to "a closer approach" to 3:1. They give no measured composition at 25 at.%.

The ~5-7 K bulk Tc therefore belongs to Ge-deficient A15 at about 18-23 at.% Ge. That is at least about 2 at.% from 25 at.%, far outside the 0.15 at.% tolerance.

A bracketing series is impossible. The bulk single-phase A15 field ends below 25 at.% Ge, so no measured single-phase bulk samples can sit on the Ge-rich side of 25 at.%.

Stoichiometric A15 Nb3Ge with Tc ~22-23 K exists only as sputtered or CVD films, and the rule excludes thin films. Stewart's review (arXiv 1505.06393, read in full text) says Nb3Ge "is unstable in bulk form and was finally stabilized at 3:1 in the A15 structure in thin film form by sputtering". As a review, that statement counts only as context, not as evidence.

Conclusion: keep the table label 'not superconducting' under the rule. The owner may still want to note that Ge-deficient bulk A15 Nb-Ge (~6-7 K) and stoichiometric Nb3Ge films (~23 K) do superconduct.

readerA.quote: "We have mapped the neutron scattering spin spectrum at low-energies in YBa2Cu3O6.353 (Tc=18 K) where the doping ~0.06 is near the critical value (pc=0.055) for superconductivity." ... "Seven ~1 cc crystals were co-aligned in the (H,H,L) scattering plane with an overall mosaic of ~1.5°. From DC magnetization (Fig. 3c) the critical temperature was measured to be Tc=18 K with a width of ~2 K."
readerA.page_table_or_figure: Title and abstract (p. 1); experimental paragraph p. 2; Fig. 3c (field-cooled DC magnetization, H//c = 1 G, Meissner transition marked Tc = 18 K). Read from arXiv cond-mat/0505083v2.
readerA.phase_or_sample: YBa2Cu3O6.353 single crystals (seven ~1 cc crystals, co-aligned), orthorhombic (a=3.843, b=3.871, c=11.788 Å), chain-oxygen order short-ranged (no superlattice peaks)
readerA.tc_criterion: Meissner transition in field-cooled DC magnetization (H//c = 1 G); Tc = 18 K with a transition width of ~2 K. The paper does not say whether this is the onset or the midpoint.
readerA.measurement_method: DC magnetization (field cooling, 1 G along c) for Tc; neutron scattering at 2-60 K
readerA.synthesis_conditions: Single crystals from the UBC group (Liang, Bonn, Hardy, who are co-authors). This paper gives no growth or annealing details. It notes the chain oxygen order is only short-ranged.
readerA.note:
Composition check: YBa2Cu3O6.353 works out to Y 0.0810, Ba 0.1619, Cu 0.2429, O 0.5143. Against our table (Y 0.081, Ba 0.162, Cu 0.244, O 0.513) the largest gap is about 0.13 at.% on O (0.130 at.% against the exact 6.32 fractions), so it is inside the 0.15 at.% limit. The pressure is not stated, but nothing suggests any was applied, so I recorded it as ambient. The Tc is the paper's own magnetization measurement, not a cited value.

I also read the lead paper in full: Manca et al., PRB 61, 15450 (2000), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.61.15450 (Crossref-verified), arXiv cond-mat/0003077. Its bulk polycrystalline k=0.32 pairs match our composition exactly (oxygen known to ±0.02 per formula unit). The text calls k=0.32 "the corresponding lower limit (k=0.32) for the existence of a partially OII-ordered superconducting phase" and notes "the coincidence of Tc in the [I] and [D] curves A4" (Fig. 1, panel A4). It never gives a Tc number, so on its own it does not meet the "with a Tc" condition.

Caveats:
- Sanna et al., PRL 93, 207001 (2004), arXiv cond-mat/0403608, lists x=0.32 at the edge of both of its ranges: samples with 0.20<=x<=0.32 never superconduct and samples with 0.32<=x<=0.42 are superconductors. Right at 6.32, whether a sample superconducts depends on how the chain oxygen is ordered and on oxygen uncertainty of about ±0.02.
- The confirmation rests on the 0.15 at.% rule as written. In oxygen per formula unit, Stock's 6.353 is 0.033 above 6.32, and YBCO's Tc changes steeply in this range.

readerA.quote: "A similar drop in Tc at x = 0.16 was also observed for y ≈ 0.53 (See Fig. 3(c)). Tc = 4 K was observed at x = 0.15 between x = 0.12 and 0.18 showing Tc max = 14 K." Also: "Using high pressure techniques, we obtained polycrystalline pellets containing >80 weight % of the 1111-type phase of SmFeAs1−yPyO1−xHx" and "Four-probe dc resistivity (ρ) and magnetic susceptibility (χ) were measured in the temperature range 2–300 K, using a physical properties measurement system (PPMS)".
readerA.page_table_or_figure: Sec. III.B (arXiv 1312.6747v1 p. 5), Fig. 3(c) resistivity and Fig. 3(f) susceptibility for y ≈ 0.53; compositions in Sec. III.A and Supplemental Fig. S1(c)
readerA.phase_or_sample: Polycrystalline pellet of 1111-type SmFeAs1-yPyO1-xHx, y ≈ 0.53 (EPMA, nominal y = 0.6), x = 0.15 (EPMA, matching the hydrogen content from TDS). Main phase >80 wt% 1111; impurities such as Fe2P present.
readerA.tc_criterion: Resistivity Tc. The paper calls Tc values the resistivity onset Tc in the same passage and notes the magnetic onset Tc_mag is slightly lower. Zero resistance is not stated for this sample.
readerA.measurement_method: Four-probe dc resistivity and VSM magnetic susceptibility in a Quantum Design PPMS, 2-300 K. No pressure cell is mentioned, so the measurements were at ambient pressure.
readerA.synthesis_conditions: Solid-state reaction of SmAs, FeAs, Fe2As, Fe2P, Sm2O3 and SmH2 in a BN capsule, with Ca(OH)2 + NaBH4 as an excess hydrogen source. Heated in a belt-type high-pressure anvil cell at 1473 K and 2 GPa for 30 min. The pressure was used only during synthesis.
readerA.note: I read the original report in full (arXiv 1312.6747v1, the preprint of the PRB paper). The DOI is registered with Crossref (Phys. Rev. B 89, 094510, 2014), and OpenAlex links it to this arXiv PDF. The paper's stated composition (y ≈ 0.53, x = 0.15, i.e. SmFeAs0.47P0.53O0.85H0.15) is the same as the table row: As 0.1175, P 0.1325, O 0.2125, H 0.0375, Sm/Fe 0.25 per atom. Caveats: (1) y ≈ 0.53 is the EPMA average for the y_nom = 0.6 series, and the per-sample y is only plotted in Fig. S1(c). (2) The pellets hold >80 wt% of the 1111 phase, not 100%. (3) This sample sits next to the Tc valley: the text says a non-superconducting region (Tc < 2 K, from magnetic onset) appears at x ≈ 0.16 in the y ≈ 0.53 series, and a drop in Tc_mag is seen at x = 0.15-0.16. Even so, the text states Tc = 4 K for x = 0.15 itself. I read the preprint, not the published PRB text, which is paywalled.

readerB.quote: "We report on nanocrystalline Nb3Ge (A15) produced by hot isostatic pressing and annealing of milled material with a bulk critical temperature and bulk upper critical field of ~12 K and ~15 T respectively." ... "EDX results for samples M6 + HIP600 and M6 + HIP1200 show a large average Cu content of ~9 at.% ... the majority phases observed in both samples are Nb3Ge, Nb5Ge3, and terminal solid solutions (Nb)ss and (Cu)ss." Conclusion: "all the materials were multiphase with copper and oxygen contamination".
readerB.page_table_or_figure: Supercond. Sci. Technol. 25 (2012) 115014: Abstract (p. 1); Table 1 (Tc = 12.0 K for M6+HIP600+A700); Fig. 3 and inset (2); EDX/XRD composition and phase text in section 3 (pp. 3-4); Conclusion (p. 5)
readerB.phase_or_sample: Bulk sample M6+HIP600+A700 (cuboid about 1 mm3) made from powders of nominal composition Nb0.75+Ge0.25. It is multiphase: A15 Nb3Ge (a = 5.153 Å), Nb5Ge3, (Nb)ss and (Cu)ss, with NbO/GeO2 and about 9 at.% Cu picked up from the milling media.
readerB.tc_criterion: Onset of the zero-field bulk diamagnetic AC-magnetization signal. A trace signal at about 17 K seen in some other samples vanished at 0.5 T.
readerB.measurement_method: AC magnetization with a Quantum Design AC magnetometer at 77 Hz, ±10 Oe, 3-20 K, in dc fields up to 8 T
readerB.synthesis_conditions: Nb and Ge powders of nominal composition Nb0.75Ge0.25 were ball-milled for 6 h with copper media in a SPEX 8000D. The powder was hot isostatically pressed for 5 h at 200 MPa and 600 °C, then annealed for 18 h at 700 °C in Ar.
readerB.note:
No paper I could read meets the rule, so the verdict is not confirmed.

(1) Best paper read (Pusceddu and Hampshire 2012). The sample is bulk, measured at ambient pressure, and has a stated Tc of 12 K. It was made from nominal Nb75Ge25, but the paper's own EDX shows about 9 at.% Cu and a multiphase sample (A15 + Nb5Ge3 + Nb and Cu solid solutions + oxides). It therefore fails the 0.15 at.% match on every element, and the Ge content of the A15 phase itself was never measured.

(2) Rathz, NASA TM-82399 (1981, full text read, no DOI). Bulk arc-cast Nb-Ge with spectroscopically measured Ge contents. Ge 22.1 at.% gives Tc 6.24 K as-cast and up to 7.29 K after drop-tube processing; Ge 27.1 at.% gives 6.04 K and 6.10 K. These samples bracket 25 at.%, but only at 2.9 and 2.1 at.%, both above the 2 at.% limit. The series is also not single-phase: equilibrium A15 sits near 20.5 at.% Ge, with Nb5Ge3 alongside.

(3) Testardi et al. 1967 (the lead, DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.154.399). Closed access; I read only the abstract. It gives Tc of about 5-7 K for V3Ge and Nb3Ge together, with no composition.

(4) Matthias et al. 1965 (DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.139.A1501). Closed access; abstract only. It says the A15 phase "normally forms with excess Nb" (Tc 6.9 K), and that rapid-quenched samples made with excess Ge reach up to 17 K. Stewart's review (arXiv 1505.06393) describes those quenched samples as nominally above 25 at.% Ge with heavy site disorder and a broad transition, and states that Nb3Ge "is unstable in bulk form" and was reached at 3:1 only in sputtered thin films.

(5) The LASL CVD Nb3Ge reports describe 3-6 µm coatings on Cu tapes, which are films and excluded.

Superconductivity is real in thin films and in Ge-poor bulk A15, but no bulk sample at Nb75Ge25 within 0.15 at.%, and no bracketing single-phase bulk series within 2 at.%, was found in a readable paper.

readerB.quote: "The oxygen content of the ellipsoid was adjusted to O6.333 by annealing at 914°C in flowing oxygen, followed by a homogenization anneal in a sealed quartz ampoule at 570°C and a quench to 0°C. At this point the sample was nonsuperconducting. After allowing chain oxygen order to develop at room temperature for three weeks, Tc was 3 K." Abstract: "measured at 2.64 GHz in highly underdoped YBa2Cu3O6+y, at 37 dopings with Tc between 3 K and 17 K."
readerB.page_table_or_figure: p. 1 (text, col. 2; abstract), PRL 99, 237003 (2007) = arXiv cond-mat/0509223v3 p. 1. Tc definition is on p. 2, Fig. 1 inset. Figs. 2, 4 and 5 show the 37 dopings.
readerB.phase_or_sample: One flux-grown YBa2Cu3O6.333 single crystal, polished into an ellipsoid 0.35 mm in diameter and 0.3 mm thick, with oxygen chain order developed at room temperature. The oxygen content stayed fixed while Tc was tuned from 3 to 17 K by chain ordering.
readerB.tc_criterion: Tc is taken from the 2.64 GHz microwave surface impedance, at the fluctuation peak (cusp) in sigma1(T). Delta Tc is the gap between the inflection points on either side of the peak, about 0.4 K. The 3 K value is the state reached by ordering at room temperature and ambient pressure only. The same O6.333 crystal reached up to 17 K after further ordering.
readerB.measurement_method: Microwave cavity perturbation at 2.64 GHz (ab-plane surface impedance) in a rutile dielectric resonator, giving the superfluid density 1/lambda^2(T) and sigma1(T).
readerB.synthesis_conditions: Single crystals were grown in BaZrO3 crucibles (high purity, cation disorder about 1e-4). The ellipsoid's oxygen was set to O6.333 at 914°C in flowing O2. It was homogenized at 570°C in a sealed quartz ampoule and quenched to 0°C, after which it was non-superconducting. Three weeks of chain ordering at room temperature gave Tc = 3 K. A further six weeks at room temperature under about 30 kbar hydrostatic pressure gave Tc = 17 K. The sample was then taken out of the pressure cell, stored at -10°C, and measured at ambient pressure. Step-wise in-situ anneals at room temperature and ambient pressure gave 36 dopings back down to 3 K. No oxygen entered or left the sample.
readerB.note:
Composition check: O6.333 has atomic fractions Y 0.08108, Ba 0.16217, Cu 0.24325, O 0.51350. Against the table row the differences are 0.009, 0.017, 0.026 and 0.051 at.%, all within 0.15. The 0.15 at.% O tolerance covers y from about 6.282 to 6.358. The text does not state the lowest measurement temperature. It must be below 3 K, since Tc = 3 K was measured and rho_s(T) is described below 4 K, so the field is null.

Lead paper: Manca et al., PRB 61, 15450 (2000), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.61.15450, Crossref-verified. I read the full text (arXiv cond-mat/0003077, p. 3, Fig. 1 panel A4). It reports bulk sintered polycrystalline k = 0.32 pairs (oxygen ±0.02) as "the corresponding lower limit (k=0.32) for the existence of a partially OII-ordered superconducting phase", with "coincidence of Tc in the [I] and [D] curves". It gives no numerical Tc in the text, so on its own it fails the stated-Tc condition.

Contrary evidence in the same window, which the rule does not weigh but is worth knowing:
- Liang et al., Physica C 383, 1 (2002), arXiv cond-mat/0111379: y = 6.340-6.345 crystals do not superconduct down to 1.5 K. Superconducting crystals start at y = 6.353 (y = 6.357 gives Tc = 9.0 K). The paper warns that absolute oxygen scales can differ by up to 0.06 between groups.
- Sanna et al., PRL 93, 207001 (2004): samples with 0.20 <= x <= 0.32 "never superconduct".

So at this composition, superconductivity depends on oxygen chain ordering and on how the oxygen scale is calibrated. The rule's first branch is still met by Broun et al.

readerB.quote: "A similar drop in Tc at x = 0.16 was also observed for y ≈ 0.53 (See Fig. 3(c)). Tc = 4 K was observed at x = 0.15 between x = 0.12 and 0.18 showing Tc^max = 14 K." Experimental: "heated at 1473 K and 2 GPa for 30 min" ... "we obtained polycrystalline pellets containing >80 weight % of the 1111-type phase" ... "Four-probe dc resistivity (ρ) and magnetic susceptibility (χ) were measured in the temperature range 2–300 K, using a physical properties measurement system (PPMS)".
readerB.page_table_or_figure: arXiv:1312.6747v1, p. 5, Sec. III.B, text on Fig. 3(c) (resistivity, y ≈ 0.53 series). Magnetic-onset data are in Fig. 3(f) and Fig. 4. Sample composition method: p. 3 (Sec. II) and Supplemental Fig. S1(c).
readerB.phase_or_sample: 1111-type SmFeAs1-yPyO1-xHx, P4/nmm. Polycrystalline high-pressure pellet, >80 wt% 1111 phase. y_EPMA ≈ 0.53 (from nominal y = 0.6) and x_EPMA = 0.15 (H content checked by TDS).
readerB.tc_criterion: Resistive transition in four-probe dc resistivity. The paper does not label the criterion for this sample. In the same paragraph, resistivity Tc values are called "onset Tc", and the magnetic onset is said to be "slightly lower than the resistivity onset Tc". Zero resistance is not stated for this sample.
readerB.measurement_method: Four-probe dc resistivity, with magnetic susceptibility from the PPMS VSM, 2–300 K at ambient pressure.
readerB.synthesis_conditions: Solid-state reaction of SmAs, FeAs, Fe2As, Fe2P, Sm2O3 and SmH2 in a belt-type high-pressure anvil cell. BN capsule with Ca(OH)2 + NaBH4 as an extra hydrogen source, held at 1473 K and 2 GPa for 30 min. The 2 GPa applies only to synthesis; measurements were at ambient pressure.
readerB.note:
Every condition of the rule is met in the paper's own text. It states Tc = 4 K for the y ≈ 0.53, x = 0.15 sample. That sample is a bulk polycrystalline pellet measured at ambient pressure, and its stated composition, SmFeAs0.47P0.53O0.85H0.15, matches our table row exactly (As 11.75, P 13.25, O 21.25, H 3.75, Sm 25, Fe 25 at.%).

Caveats for the adjudicator:
(1) The paper conflicts with itself on this sample. About the magnetic-onset plot (Fig. 4) it says "the non-SC region (Tc < 2 K) was found at x ≈ 0.16 in the y ≈ 0.53 series", and that a drop of Tc^mag was seen at x = 0.15–0.16. The valley sample in this series is the x = 0.15 one, so its diamagnetic onset may be below 2 K. If so, the 4 K Tc is resistive only, with no Meissner signal shown above 2 K. I could not view the figures to settle this.
(2) Zero resistance is not stated for this sample.
(3) In the x = 0 sample of the same series, the authors attribute a resistivity drop near 5 K to Sm3+ antiferromagnetic ordering, not superconductivity. They do not apply that reading to the x = 0.15 sample.
(4) y ≈ 0.53 is an EPMA value for the whole series, not a number given for this sample. The match is exact to the stated composition, but its precision is about ±0.01 in y.
(5) I read the full text of arXiv v1. The published PRB version, revised 10 Feb 2014, and its supplement are paywalled and were not read. Crossref confirms the DOI.

A reader who requires bulk diamagnetism, or who counts the "non-SC region" sentence as the paper's verdict on this sample, could reasonably rate it "cannot tell".

verified.quote: "We report on nanocrystalline Nb3Ge (A15) produced by hot isostatic pressing and annealing of milled material with a bulk critical temperature and bulk upper critical field of ~12 K and ~15 T respectively. Optimum macroscopic bulk critical values were only produced in a narrow window of processing parameters: mechanically alloyed Nb0.75 + Ge0.25 milled for 6 or 20 h was processed in a hot isostatic press for 5 h operating at 2000 bar and 600 °C followed by annealing at 700 °C for 18 h." ... the best materials "consist of very weakly coupled islands of nanocrystalline material with critical temperatures up to ~17 K in a resistive grain boundary matrix"
verified.page_table_or_figure: Supercond. Sci. Technol. 25 (2012) 115014, abstract (I read it via OpenAlex). Reader B read the full text and cites Table 1 (Tc 12.0 K for M6+HIP600+A700), Fig. 3, and the EDX/XRD section (pp. 3-4) for about 9 at.% Cu and a multiphase sample. The full text is closed access and I could not reach it.
verified.phase_or_sample: Bulk nanocrystalline material, HIP'd and annealed, made from milled powders of NOMINAL Nb0.75Ge0.25. A15 Nb3Ge islands sit in a resistive grain-boundary matrix. Per Reader B's full-text read, the sample is multiphase (A15 + Nb5Ge3 + (Nb)ss + (Cu)ss + oxides) with about 9 at.% Cu from the milling media. The A15 phase's own Ge content was never analysed.
verified.pressure: ambient (measurement); 2000 bar applied only during HIP synthesis
verified.tc_criterion: Bulk-screening (AC susceptibility) critical temperature of about 12 K, from the abstract. Small zero-field screening signals near 17 K in a few samples collapsed at 0.5 T.
verified.measurement_method: AC susceptibility with a commercial AC susceptometer (abstract). Reader B, from the full text: Quantum Design ACMS, 77 Hz, 3-20 K, dc fields up to 8 T.
verified.synthesis_conditions: Mechanical alloying of nominal Nb0.75+Ge0.25 for 6 or 20 h, then HIP for 5 h at 2000 bar and 600 °C, then annealing for 18 h at 700 °C (abstract). Reader B, from the full text: SPEX mill with Cu media, which is the source of the Cu contamination.
verified.note:
Final: do not apply. Both readers returned "not confirmed", and the rule applies a correction only when both confirm. My own checks found nothing that meets either branch of the rule, so I agree with both readers.

(1) Pusceddu & Hampshire 2012 (Crossref-verified). The sample is bulk and was measured at ambient pressure, with a stated Tc of ~12 K. But 75/25 is only the nominal powder composition. The paper describes a multiphase material (A15 islands in a resistive matrix; Reader B's full-text read adds ~9 at.% Cu, Nb5Ge3, solid solutions and oxides). That fails the 0.15 at.%-on-every-element test.

(2) Matthias et al. 1965 (DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.139.A1501; abstract read via OpenAlex). The A15 phase "normally forms with excess Nb" with Tc 6.9 K. Rapid-quenched samples made with excess Ge reach "as high as 17 K", which the authors attribute to "a closer approach" to 3:1. The abstract gives no measured composition at 25.0 at.% Ge.

(3) Testardi et al. 1967 (DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.154.399, Crossref-verified, closed access). The abstract gives only a shared ~5-7 K for V3Ge and Nb3Ge, with no composition.

(4) Jorda, Flukiger & Muller 1978 (DOI 10.1016/0022-5088(78)90013-9). The OpenAlex record exists but has no abstract. The readers' ScienceDirect quote says the bulk Ge-rich limit is 20-23 +/- 1 at.% Ge, and that "the stoichiometric composition Nb3Ge is not reached". If that holds, no single-phase bulk series can bracket 25 at.% from the Ge-rich side, so the second branch of the rule fails too.

(5) Rathz, NASA TM-82399 (from Reader B; I did not re-read it). The samples bracket 25 at.% only at 2.9 and 2.1 at.%, both outside the 2 at.% limit, and the series is not single-phase.
verified.refutation_attempt:
Both readers rejected the correction, so I also looked for evidence that would support it, a bulk stoichiometric Nb3Ge.

What I did: checked both DOIs in Crossref (Testardi 1967, Pusceddu 2012); read the OpenAlex abstracts of Matthias 1965 and Pusceddu 2012; checked the Jorda 1978 record (no abstract in OpenAlex). I then searched for bulk, shock-synthesised, explosively compressed and high-pressure Nb3Ge. The only explosive-compression A15 hit was Nb3Si (DOI 10.1088/1361-648X/abeace), not Nb3Ge.

The strongest lead was Newkirk, Valencia, Giorgi, Szklarz & Wallace, 'Bulk superconductivity above 20 K in Nb3Ge', IEEE Trans. Magn. 11, 221 (1975), DOI 10.1109/TMAG.1975.1058637. I read the full text of the LASL preprint on OSTI (purl 4244932). It still fails the rule in three ways:
(a) The samples are a "bulk film (0.02-0.06 mm thick) of Nb3Ge deposited on Cu substrates by chemical vapor deposition", i.e. a CVD coating bonded to a substrate, not a free-standing polycrystal or single crystal.
(b) No composition is measured. Tc is related only to the lattice parameter (Fig. 7).
(c) The paper says the best (Tc 20-21 K) material is "not single phase A-15 material, but may contain anywhere from 5-20% of the compound Nb5Ge3", and single-phase A15 "has been produced but thus far only for lower Tc material".

None of this refutes the readers. Every superconducting sample found sits in one of three groups: Ge-deficient bulk A15 at about 18-23 at.% Ge (6-7 K); quenched, multiphase or contaminated bulk with only a nominal composition; or films and coatings. No paper I could read shows a bulk sample within 0.15 at.% of Nb75Ge25, or a single-phase bulk series that brackets it within 2 at.%.

verified.quote: "The oxygen content of the ellipsoid was adjusted to O6.333 by annealing at 914 °C in flowing oxygen, followed by a homogenization anneal in a sealed quartz ampoule at 570 °C and a quench to 0 °C. At this point the sample was nonsuperconducting. After allowing chain oxygen order to develop at room temperature for three weeks, Tc was 3 K." ... "periods of controlled in-situ annealing at room temperature and ambient pressure were used to generate a sequence of 36 dopings as Tc relaxed back to 3 K. We emphasize that no oxygen entered or left the sample during these annealing steps." Abstract: "measured at 2.64 GHz in highly underdoped YBa2Cu3O6+y, at 37 dopings with Tc between 3 K and 17 K."
verified.page_table_or_figure: PRL 99, 237003 (2007), read as arXiv cond-mat/0509223v3. The abstract and sample preparation are on p. 1, col. 2. The Tc definition is on p. 2 (Fig. 1 inset, the sigma1 fluctuation peak). Fig. 2 shows the sequence down to Tc ≈ 3 K, and Figs. 4 and 5 show Tc versus doping. Also checked: Stock et al., PRB 73, 100504 (2006), arXiv cond-mat/0505083v2, p. 2 and Fig. 3c (YBa2Cu3O6.353, Tc = 18 K from field-cooled DC magnetization).
verified.phase_or_sample: One flux-grown YBa2Cu3O6.333 single crystal grown in a BaZrO3 crucible, cut and polished into an ellipsoid 0.35 mm in diameter and 0.3 mm thick. It is orthorhombic YBCO, with Tc tuned by room-temperature CuO-chain ordering at a fixed oxygen content. It is a bulk crystal, not a film.
verified.tc_criterion: Tc is the cusp, or fluctuation peak, in the 2.64 GHz ab-plane microwave conductivity sigma1(T). The width Delta Tc ≈ 0.4 K is the gap between the sigma1 inflection points. The 3 K value belongs to the state reached by room-temperature chain ordering at ambient pressure only.
verified.measurement_method: Microwave cavity perturbation at 2.64 GHz (ab-plane surface impedance Zs, in a rutile dielectric resonator with a sapphire hot finger), giving sigma1(T) and the superfluid density 1/lambda^2(T).
verified.synthesis_conditions: Single crystals were grown in BaZrO3 crucibles, with cation disorder at about 1e-4. Oxygen was set to O6.333 at 914 °C in flowing O2, then homogenized at 570 °C in a sealed quartz ampoule and quenched to 0 °C, after which the crystal was non-superconducting. Three weeks of room-temperature chain ordering gave Tc = 3 K. A later 6-week room-temperature anneal under about 30 kbar raised Tc to 17 K. The pressure was then removed and the sample stored at -10 °C. Measurements were made at ambient pressure, with in-situ ambient-pressure anneals stepping Tc back down to 3 K. No oxygen entered or left the sample.
verified.note:
I read both readers' papers in full and checked both DOIs against Crossref (PRL 99, 237003, Broun et al. 2007; PRB 73, 100504, Stock et al. 2006).

Composition:
- O6.333 gives Y 0.08108, Ba 0.16217, Cu 0.24325, O 0.51350. Exact 6.32 gives Y 0.08117, Ba 0.16234, Cu 0.24351, O 0.51299. The differences are 0.009, 0.017, 0.026 and 0.051 at.%. Against the rounded key the largest gap is 0.075 at.% on Cu.
- Stock's O6.353 is within 0.130 at.% on O and 0.114 at.% on Cu against the key, so it also passes, but less comfortably.
- I chose Broun as the best evidence for two reasons. Its composition is closer. Its 3 K state was reached by ambient-pressure room-temperature ordering alone, so pressure cannot be an issue, even though other states in the paper were pressure-annealed and only measured at ambient.

Stock et al.: seven ~1 cc single crystals with Tc = 18 K and a ~2 K width from field-cooled DC magnetization (H//c = 1 G). The paper's own measurement shows a sharp Meissner transition. No pressure is mentioned and the measurement was at 2 K and above.

The lowest measurement temperature in Broun is not stated. It must be below 3 K, because Tc ≈ 3 K was resolved and rho_s is described below 4 K.

Caveat: superconductivity at y ≈ 6.32-6.35 depends on chain-oxygen ordering. Broun's own crystal was non-superconducting right after the quench. Contrary reports exist (Liang et al. 2002: y = 6.340-6.345 non-superconducting; Sanna et al. 2004: x ≤ 0.32 never superconducts), and oxygen scales differ between groups. The owner's rule does not weigh contrary reports, and the first branch of the rule is met.
verified.refutation_attempt:
I tried six ways to refute the correction:
1. Thin film or heterostructure: no. Broun used a single polished bulk crystal ellipsoid, and Stock used seven ~1 cc co-aligned single crystals.
2. Pressure: Broun pressure-annealed at ~30 kbar for the higher-Tc states, but every measurement was at ambient pressure. The 3 K state at fixed O6.333 came only from room-temperature ordering at ambient pressure, both at the start and again at the end of the in-situ relaxation sequence. Stock mentions no pressure.
3. Composition outside 0.15 at.%: I recomputed it. Broun's largest gap is 0.05 at.% on O, or 0.075 at.% on Cu against the rounded key. Stock's largest is 0.13 at.% on O. Both pass.
4. Cited rather than measured Tc: no. Both Tc values are the papers' own measurements (Broun by microwave sigma1, Stock in Fig. 3c by DC magnetization). Broun's Fig. 3 Tc(p) data from Ref. 13 is cited, but it is not the value used here.
5. Different phase: no. Both samples are orthorhombic YBa2Cu3O6+y with short-range chain order.
6. Misread figure or text: no. The quoted text says it directly: "Tc was 3 K" at O6.333, and "Tc=18 K" for YBa2Cu3O6.353.

The only weakness is physical, not a rule failure: the composition sits at the superconducting boundary, where Tc depends on chain ordering and on how the oxygen scale is calibrated. I could not refute the correction.

The paper's magnetic-onset summary (Fig. 4 and its text) puts the y ≈ 0.53 valley at x ≈ 0.16 in a "non-SC region (Tc < 2 K)". So no diamagnetic Tc above 2 K is reported for this point.

verified.synthesis_conditions: Solid-state reaction of SmAs, FeAs, Fe2As, Fe2P, Sm2O3 and SmH2 in a BN capsule, with Ca(OH)2 + NaBH4 as an excess hydrogen source. Heated in a belt-type high-pressure anvil cell at 1473 K and 2 GPa for 30 min. The pressure applies only to synthesis.
verified.note:
I read the full text of arXiv 1312.6747v1 myself. The rest of the published record is consistent with it. Crossref registers the DOI (PRB 89, 094510, 2014), and OpenAlex links it to this arXiv PDF. An arXiv v2 is listed but has no PDF, and the published PRB text and its supplement are paywalled, so I did not read them.

Both readers quoted the paper accurately, and the bulk-sample, ambient-pressure and stated-composition conditions hold. The correction fails on the core condition: the paper's own text does not clearly state superconductivity for this composition.
(1) The y ≈ 0.53 samples the text names around the valley are x = 0.12, 0.15 and 0.18. The authors loosely call the valley "x = 0.16" ("a similar drop in Tc at x = 0.16 was also observed for y ≈ 0.53", then "Tc = 4 K was observed at x = 0.15"). They place the Tc^mag drop at "x = 0.15–0.16 for y ≈ 0.45 and 0.53". They then classify the y ≈ 0.53 point at "x ≈ 0.16" as "the non-SC region (Tc < 2 K)". The most direct reading is that the x = 0.15 sample is that non-SC point in the magnetic phase diagram.
(2) The paper says χ-T data show "bulk superconductivity". By that test, this sample shows none above 2 K.
(3) For the x = 0 sample of the same series, the authors attribute a ~5 K resistivity drop with no susceptibility drop to Sm3+ antiferromagnetic order, not superconductivity. The 4 K resistive feature here, with no stated zero resistance and no diamagnetic onset above 2 K, meets the same description. The authors do not apply that reading to it, but they do not rule it out either.
(4) The composition is approximate. y ≈ 0.53 is a series average, and the per-sample y is only plotted in Fig. S1(c). The 0.15 at.% tolerance on P means |Δy| ≤ 0.006, which "≈ 0.53" does not guarantee.

The bracketing route does not rescue the correction. The measured neighbours x = 0.12 and 0.18 are superconducting (Tc max 14 K), but the paper itself reports a non-SC (Tc < 2 K) point between them at the target. So the series around this composition is not "all superconducting".

The existing "not superconducting" label is consistent with the paper's own magnetic-onset phase diagram. I could not view Figs. 3(c), 3(f) and 4 to settle this directly. Until someone reads those figures, or the PRB supplement, and shows a diamagnetic or zero-resistance transition at x = 0.15, the evidence is in conflict and the correction should not be applied.
verified.refutation_attempt:
I checked each condition against the full text.
- Bulk: met (polycrystalline pellets).
- Ambient pressure: met (2 GPa only during synthesis; PPMS measurements with no pressure cell).
- Composition: matches the stated y ≈ 0.53, x = 0.15 exactly, though y is a series average.
- Measured vs cited: the Tc is this paper's own measurement.
- Superconductivity: refuted as unambiguous. The only support is a resistive 4 K Tc, with no zero resistance stated and data only down to 2 K. The same section says the y ≈ 0.53 series has a "non-SC region (Tc < 2 K)" at x ≈ 0.16. That is the Tc valley, and the text identifies the valley sample as x = 0.15, between neighbours at 0.12 and 0.18. So the paper's magnetic phase diagram (Fig. 4) classifies this sample as non-superconducting above 2 K.
- The authors' own rule in the same series is that a low-T resistivity drop with no susceptibility drop is Sm3+ AFM order (x = 0, ≈ 5 K). That rule casts doubt on the 4 K feature.
- Both readers flagged this conflict themselves.
- Bracketing route: fails, because a reported non-SC point lies inside the bracket.
Verdict: cannot tell. The correction should not be applied.
